title: Lupinus angustifolius
wikitext:
{{Short description|Species of legume}} {{Speciesbox |image = Lupinus angustifolius 20150331 a.jpg |image2 = |genus = Lupinus |species = angustifolius |authority = [[Carl Linnaeus|L.]] }} [[File:Lupinus angustifolius MHNT.BOT.2016.24.52.jpg|thumb|''Lupinus angustifolius'' - [[MHNT]]]] '''''Lupinus angustifolius''''' is a species of [[lupin]] known by many common names, including '''narrowleaf lupin''',{{PLANTS|id=LUAN4|taxon=Lupinus angustifolius|accessdate=27 January 2016}} '''narrow-leaved lupin'''{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }} and '''blue lupin'''. It is native to Eurasia and northern Africa and naturalized in parts of Australia and North America. It has been cultivated for over 6000 years{{cite book | last =Gladstones | first =J.S. |author2=Atkins, Hamblin | title =Lupins as crop plants | publisher =CAB International | year =1998 | location =Wallingford, Oxon, UK | page =353 | isbn =0-85199-224-2 }} as a food crop for its edible [[legume]] seeds, as a [[fodder]] for livestock and for [[green manure]]. ==Biology== Like other legumes, the narrow-leaved lupin [[nitrogen fixation|fixes nitrogen]] in a symbiotic interaction with different bacteria in the [[rhizosphere]]. Bacteria living in this rhizosphere include ''Bradyrhizobium lupinii'' or the newly discovered species ''Kribbella lupini''.Trujillo, M. E., et al. (2006). [http://ijs.sgmjournals.org/cgi/reprint/56/2/407 ''Kribbella lupini'' sp. nov., isolated from the roots of ''Lupinus angustifolius''] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080607015535/http://ijs.sgmjournals.org/cgi/reprint/56/2/407 |date=2008-06-07 }}. ''Int J Syst Evol Microbiol'' 56:407-11. In some places these bacteria are not native to the soil and need to be inocculated onto the seed for the lupins to have a nitrogen fixing effect.{{Cite web |title=Merkblatt Lupinen|url=https://www.strickhof.ch/publikationen/merkblatt-lupinen/|access-date=2025-11-06|website=Strickhof|language=de}} It was found that Lupins accumulate on average 195.4 kg N/h, 80 % of which were fixed from the atmosphere.{{Cite journal |last1=Natera|first1=Juan Francisco Zamora|last2=Hernández|first2=Isidro Zapata|last3=Jiménez|first3=Carlos Ernesto Aguilar|last4=Aguilar|first4=Franklin B. Martínez|last5=Galdámez|first5=José Galdámez|date=2023-09-27|title=Assessing the biomass yield and nitrogen fixation of Lupinus angustifolius varieties as green manure in Jalisco, Mexico|url=https://dergipark.org.tr/en/pub/ejss/issue/77854/1328548|journal=Eurasian Journal of Soil Science|language=en|volume=12|issue=4|pages=320–327|doi=10.18393/ejss.1328548|issn=2147-4249}}
The narrow-leaved lupin is an erect, branching [[herb]] sometimes exceeding one meter. There are reduced-branching cultivars. Each palmate leaf is divided into 5 to 9 linear leaflets under 4 centimeters long. The herbage is slightly hairy in some areas. The [[inflorescence]] bears many flowers in shades of blue, violet, pink, or white. The fruit is a legume pod containing seeds of varying colors from dark gray to brown to white, or speckled or mottled.{{cite web|last=FAO, Food and Agriculture Organization of the UN|title=Lupinus angustifolius|url=http://ecocrop.fao.org/ecocrop/srv/en/cropView?id=2519|access-date=29 November 2012}} Lupinus angustifolius has a high content of alkaloids, e.g. lupanin or angustifolin. However, cultivars with a low alkaloid content have been bred. These low alkaloid cultivars are called sweet lupins, such as the ''Australian Sweet Lupin''.{{Cite web |last=Nicholas |first=Lorna |date=2020-05-18 |title=Wide Open Agriculture enters multi-billion-dollar plant-based protein market |url=https://smallcaps.com.au/wide-open-agriculture-enters-multi-billion-dollar-plant-based-protein-market/ |access-date=2021-02-27 |website=Small Caps}} File:Lupinus angustifolius FlowersCloseup 2009Mach28 DehesaBoyaldePuertollano.jpg File:Lupinus angustifolius3.jpg == Domestication and Modern Use == The process of domestication for narrow-leaved lupine presumably started in the 1930‒1940s, when the discovered alkaloid-free mutants enabled plant breeders in Germany and Sweden to develop the first forage cultivars.Vishnyakova MA, Vlasova EV, Egorova GP. Genetic resources of narrow-leaved lupine (Lupinus angustifolius L.) and their role in its domestication and breeding. Vavilovskii Zhurnal Genet Selektsii. 2021 Oct;25(6):620–30. The first fully domesticated varieties of L. angustifolius were developed in the 1960s by John Gladstones at the [[University of Western Australia]]. Subsequently, the Australian sweet and non-shattering L. angustifolius genetics has been utilised by plant breeders in [[Germany]], [[Poland]], [[Belarus]] and [[Russia]] to breed sweet grain varieties suitable for northern European conditions, including enhanced flowering time regulation, more uniform maturation, greater tolerance to cooler environments, and resistance to fungal diseases.Gresta F, Wink M, Prins U, Abberton M, Capraro J, Scarafoni A, et al. Lupins in European cropping systems. In: Legumes in cropping systems [Internet]. 2017 [cited 2025 Nov 30]. p. 88–108. (CABI Books). Available from: https://www.cabidigitallibrary.org/doi/abs/10.1079/9781780644981.0088 [[Australia]] adopted the common name 'Australian sweet lupin' to emphasise that Australian narrow-leafed lupin has [[alkaloid]] levels within the [[Food Standards Australia and New Zealand]] standard of seed with 0.02% total [[alkaloids]] or below.{{Cite web| title=Lupins – Botany and Global Use in Agriculture | url=https://aussielupins.org.au/wp-content/uploads/bsk-pdf-manager/2023/08/Lupin_BotanyGlobal_use_in_Agriculture.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240318211126/https://aussielupins.org.au/wp-content/uploads/bsk-pdf-manager/2023/08/Lupin_BotanyGlobal_use_in_Agriculture.pdf | archive-date=2024-03-18}} Blue Lupin production expanded rapidly in [[Western Australia]] through the 1980s and 1990s, but persistent weed problems and declining market prices made lupin cultivation less profitable and more difficult to manage. Consequently, many growers switched to [[canola]] (or [[fallow]]), leading to a sharp drop in production from a peak of 1.5 million tonnes in 1999 to just under 300,000 tonnes in 2012.Lupins [Internet]. 2024 [cited 2025 Nov 30]. Available from: https://www.dpird.wa.gov.au/businesses/plant-and-crop-farming/grains/lupins/ In 2023, [[Western Australia]] produced 400,000 tonnes of blue lupin.Lupins [Internet]. 2024 [cited 2025 Nov 9]. Available from: https://www.dpird.wa.gov.au/businesses/plant-and-crop-farming/grains/lupins/ In [[Poland]], the second largest producer of lupins after [[Australia]], narrow-leaved lupins have gained importance in recent years.FAOSTAT [Internet]. [cited 2025 Nov 9]. Available from: https://www.fao.org/faostat/en/#data/QCL/visualizeClements J, Galek R, Kozak B, Michalczyk DJ, Piotrowicz-Cieślak AI, Sawicka-Sienkiewicz E, et al. Diversity of Selected Lupinus angustifolius L. Genotypes at the Phenotypic and DNA Level with Respect to Microscopic Seed Coat Structure and Thickness. PLOS ONE. 2014 Aug 13;9(8):e102874. In [[Russia]], the area cultivated with narrow-leaved lupins reached 78,971 hectares in 2019.Vishnyakova MA, Vlasova EV, Egorova GP. Genetic resources of narrow-leaved lupine (Lupinus angustifolius L.) and their role in its domestication and breeding. Vavilovskii Zhurnal Genet Selektsii. 2021 Oct;25(6):620–30. ==Agronomy== The narrow-leaved lupin is sown as early as possible in the spring,{{cite journal|last=Eckardt|first=Thomas |author2=Haag, Franz |author3=Dietrich, Regine|title=Der Einfluss von Wuchstyp, Saatzeitpunkt und Saatstärke auf den Kornertrag von Blauen Süsslupinen (Lupinus angustifolius)|journal=Lupinen 2001:Ergebnisse aus Forschung, Anbau und Verwertung|year=2002}} to have the growing season as long as possible. Another reason for early sowing is its sensitivity to high temperature in spring.{{cite book | last =Gladstones | first =J.S. |author2=Atkins, Hamblin | title =Lupins as crop plants | publisher =CAB International | year =1998 | location =Wallingford, Oxon, UK | page =304 | isbn =0-85199-224-2 }} Lupins react with a higher yield loss, when they are sown late, than other crops (e.g. cereals) do.{{cite book | last =Gladstones | first =J.S. |author2=Atkins, Hamblin | title =Lupins as crop plants | publisher =CAB International | year =1998 | location =Wallingford, Oxon, UK | page =303 | isbn =0-85199-224-2 }} The optimum seed density depends on the site yield potential {{cite book | last =Gladstones | first =J.S. |author2=Atkins, Hamblin | title =Lupins as crop plants | publisher =CAB International | year =1998 | location =Wallingford, Oxon, UK | pages =304–307 | isbn =0-85199-224-2 }} and is generally higher in non-branching cultivars than in branching ones. The variance is high, 14 to 138 plants per m2{{cite journal|last=French|first=R.J. |author2=McCarthy, K. |author3=Smart, W.L.|title=Optimum plant population densities for lupin (Lupinus angustifolius L.) in the wheatbelt of Western Australia|journal=Australian Journal of Experimental Agriculture|year=1994|volume=34|issue=4 |pages=491–497|doi=10.1071/EA9940491}} are an optimal plant density, depending on the yield potential of the site. On most grounds, a plant density around 80 plants per m2 would be the optimum. Lupins are usually sown with technique used for [[cereals]] in a depth of about 5 cm. The narrow-leaved lupin needs to be harvested as soon as the grain reaches a moisture of about 12%. The [[straw]] usually isn't ripened at this point, but further delay of harvest would increase losses from shattering of the pods and [[lodging (agriculture)|lodging]].{{cite book | last =Gladstones | first =J.S. |author2=Atkins, Hamblin | title =Lupins as crop plants | publisher =CAB International | year =1998 | location =Wallingford, Oxon, UK | page =320 | isbn =0-85199-224-2 }} The harvest is done with machinery used for cereals. [[Swathing]] is not widely applied. However, it can be a good alternative to reduce harvest losses in case harvest is delayed. The disease and weed spectrum of the narrow-leaved lupin is different from most major crops and it is able to improve the [[soil]] (see Use). Therefore, it is a valuable partner in intensive [[crop rotation]]s. In the main cultivation area in [[Australia]] lupin yields typically reach 3-3.5 t/ha.{{Cite web|title=Lupin|url=https://www.dpi.nsw.gov.au/dpi/climate/climate-vulnerability-assessment/broadacre-cropping/lupin|website=DPI Website|date=2025-06-30|access-date=2025-11-30|language=en-AU}} Yields in [[Europe]] are less stable. They range from 2-4 t/ha.{{Cite web |title=Merkblatt Lupinen|url=https://www.strickhof.ch/publikationen/merkblatt-lupinen/|access-date=2025-11-06|website=Strickhof|language=de}} The reasons for which are mainly environmental. With higher rainfalls being disadvantageous for a successful lupin cultivation {{Cite journal|title=Insights from the yield, protein production, and detailed alkaloid composition of white (Lupinus albus), narrow-leafed (Lupinus angustifolius), and yellow (Lupinus luteus) lupin cultivars in the Mediterranean region|journal=Frontiers in Plant Science|date=2023-12-15|issn=1664-462X|pmc=10755673|pmid=38162308|volume=14|doi=10.3389/fpls.2023.1231777|language=English|first1=Inês M.|last1=Valente|first2=Carla|last2=Sousa|first3=Mariana|last3=Almeida|first4=Carla|last4=Miranda|first5=Victor|last5=Pinheiro|first6=Sofia|last6=Garcia-Santos|first7=Luís M. M.|last7=Ferreira|first8=Cristina M.|last8=Guedes|first9=Margarida R. G.|last9=Maia|first10=Ana R. J.|last10=Cabrita|first11=António J. M.|last11=Fonseca|first12=Henrique|last12=Trindade |article-number=1231777 |bibcode=2023FrPS...1431777V |doi-access=free }} == Pests and Diseases == ''L. angustifolius'' is affected by various insect pests, viral diseases and fungal pathogens, which can negatively affect the final yield. Narrow-leaved lupin plants synthesize [[quinolizidine alkaloids]] (QAs) as [[Secondary metabolite|secondary metabolites]] within their leaves {{Cite journal |last1=Wink|first1=Michael|last2=Meißner|first2=Carsten|last3=Witte|first3=Ludger|date=January 1995|title=Patterns of quinolizidine alkaloids in 56 species of the genus Lupinus|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/003194229591890D|journal=Phytochemistry|language=en|volume=38|issue=1|pages=139–153|doi=10.1016/0031-9422(95)91890-D |bibcode=1995PChem..38..139W }} to protect themselves against herbivores, but a few insect species have adapted to tolerate those substances.{{Cite journal |last1=Piedra-García|first1=Diego|last2=Struck|first2=Christine|date=2021-10-18|title=Lupin Root Weevils (Charagmus spp., Curculionidae: Sitonini), a Lupin Pest: A Review of Their Distribution, Biology, and Challenges in Integrated Pest Management|journal=Insects|language=en|volume=12|issue=10|page=950|doi=10.3390/insects12100950|doi-access=free |issn=2075-4450|pmc=8540778|pmid=34680719}}{{Citation |last1=Brown |first1=Keith S. |last2=Trigo |first2=José Roberto |title=Chapter 4 The Ecological Activity of Alkaloids|date=1995-01-01|series=The Alkaloids: Chemistry and Pharmacology |volume=47|pages=227–354|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/chapter/bookseries/abs/pii/S009995980860156X|access-date=2025-11-06|publisher=Academic Press|language=en-US|doi=10.1016/s0099-9598(08)60156-x |isbn=978-0-12-469547-4 }} === Insect pests === [[Lupin Root Weevil|Lupin Root Weevils]] (''Charagmus'' spp., [[Curculionidae]]: [[Sitonini]]) are species of beetles widely spread in Europe that can be very damaging to lupin plants. The adult beetles feed on the leaves of the crop, usually not causing significant damage. The most damaging are the larvae of lupin root weevils that can infect and feed on the [[Root nodule|root nodules]].{{Cite journal |last=Ferguson|first=Andrew W.|date=1994-05-01|title=Pests and plant injury on lupins in the south of England|journal=Crop Protection|volume=13|issue=3|pages=201–210|doi=10.1016/0261-2194(94)90079-5|bibcode=1994CrPro..13..201F |issn=0261-2194}} The damage to roots can reduce the plant's ability to fix nitrogen and it also enables soil pathogens to enter the roots. Lupin root weevils can be controlled through chemical control, tillage and use of [[Biological pest control|biological control agents]]. The lupin aphid (''[[Macrosiphum albifrons]]'') have evolved to tolerate QAs and feed on high-alkaloid lupins, while other [[aphid]] species mostly feed on sweet lupin cultivars with low alkaloid content. Lupin plants are most vulnerable to ''M. albifrons'' during the budding and flowering stage.{{Cite journal|title=Managing aphids and viruses in lupins|url=https://library.dpird.wa.gov.au/fc_factsheets/28|journal=Grains and Other Field Crops Factsheets|date=2024-09-01|last=Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development, Western Australia}} Heavy infestations during flowering can cause poor pod set or, in severe cases, no development of pods. Control methods include [[Insecticide|insecticides]], high sowing densities and narrow row spacing to discourage aphid landing, and [[Biological pest control|biological control]]. However, chemical control is often not economical and biocontrol agents can effectively control aphid populations only under low to moderate infestation levels.{{Cite book |last1=French |first1=R.J. |title=Encyclopedia of Food Grains |date=2016-01-01|chapter=Lupin: Agronomy|chapter-url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/chapter/referencework/abs/pii/B9780123944375001947|language=en-US|pages=231–239|doi=10.1016/B978-0-12-394437-5.00194-7 |isbn=978-0-12-394786-4 }} === Viral diseases === ''M. albifrons'' and other aphids are a vector of [[bean yellow mosaic virus]] (BYMV) and [[cucumber mosaic virus]] (CMV). CMV can be seed-borne in narrow-leaved lupin, meaning the virus can infect developing seeds and survive in them for a long time.{{Cite journal|title=Transmission through seeds: The unknown life of plant viruses|journal=PLOS Pathogens|date=2022-08-11|issn=1553-7374|pmc=9371277|pmid=35951532|article-number=e1010707|volume=18|issue=8|doi=10.1371/journal.ppat.1010707|language=en|first=Israel|last=Pagán | doi-access=free }} The plants that grow from such seeds will also be infected and serve as sources of further disease spread via [[Aphid|aphids]]. BYMV is not seed-borne in the narrow-leaved lupin and can only be transmitted by aphids feeding on already infected plants. Because both diseases are mostly transmitted by aphids, controlling aphid populations and removing weeds from which the aphids can acquire the disease can help control CMV and BYMV. Spread of seed-borne CMV can be minimized by using certified virus-free seeds. === Fungal pathogens === Narrow-leafed lupin can be affected by lupin [[anthracnose]], a major fungal disease caused by the pathogenic fungus ''[[Colletotrichum lini|Colletotrichum lupini]]''. The disease can lead to substantial yield losses.{{Cite journal |last1=Alkemade|first1=Joris A.|last2=Patyi|first2=András|last3=Arncken|first3=Christine|last4=Lazzaro|first4=Mariateresa|date=2025-04-11|title=Lupins: A Remarkable Protein Crop Battling Anthracnose for a Greener Future|url=https://www.cabidigitallibrary.org/doi/full/10.1079/planthealthcases.2025.0008|journal=Plant Health Cases|volume=2025|article-number=phcs20250008|doi=10.1079/planthealthcases.2025.0008}} The pathogen is transmitted primarily through affected seeds, but is also spread within the field by spores dispersed by rain splash from lesions on infected plants. Typical symptoms include twisting and bending of stems and in later stages [[Necrosis|necrotic]] lesions. The use of disease-free seed is a key management practice, although even very low levels of seed [[infection]] (as little as 0.01%) can already cause the disease. [[Fungicide|Fungicides]] can be used to control the disease through [[Seed treatment|seed coating]] or foliar application. The most promising way of combating anthracnose in lupin is using resistant varieties, which can achieve as much as double the yield as susceptible varieties. Several single dominant [[Resistance gene|resistance genes]] have been identified and there are resistant varieties, such as 'Tanjil' and 'Mandelup', available.{{Cite journal |last1=Książkiewicz|first1=Michał|last2=Rychel-Bielska|first2=Sandra|last3=Plewiński|first3=Piotr|last4=Bielski|first4=Wojciech|last5=Nuc|first5=Maria|last6=Kozak|first6=Bartosz|last7=Krajewski|first7=Paweł|last8=Jędryczka|first8=Małgorzata|date=2022-05-17|title=A successful defense of the narrow-leafed lupin against anthracnose involves quick and orchestrated reprogramming of oxidation–reduction, photosynthesis and pathogenesis-related genes|journal=Scientific Reports|language=en|volume=12|issue=1|article-number=8164 |doi=10.1038/s41598-022-12257-7 |doi-access=free|issn=2045-2322|pmc=9114385|pmid=35581248 |bibcode=2022NatSR..12.8164K }} ==Use== The plant is used as a [[green manure]] or as a grain legume for animal feed or human consumption. Through its ability to fix nitrogen and its low nutrient requirement this plant is suitable to be planted on exhausted fields as a [[soil improver]]. Additionally, lupins have strong roots, that can reduce the [[soil compaction|compaction of a soil]].{{cite journal|last=Henderson|first=C.W.L.|title=Using a penetrometer to predict the effects of soil compaction on the growth and yield of wheat on uniform sandy soils.|journal=Australian Journal of Agricultural Research|year=1989|volume=40|issue=3|pages=497–5008|doi=10.1071/AR9890497}} The whole plant, including the seeds, is widely used as a fodder for livestock, due to its high [[protein]] and energy content. Lupins contain high levels of fermentable carbohydrates and low levels of [[starch]] and are, therefore, an adequate [[ruminant]] feed. But lupins are a valuable feed for [[monogastric]] animals as well, because of the high [[digestibility]] of the lupin nitrogen and the low level of [[protease inhibitors]].Heuzé V., Thiollet H., Tran G., Lessire M., Lebas F., 2018. Blue lupin (Lupinus angustifolius) seeds. Feedipedia, a programme by INRA, CIRAD, AFZ and FAO. https://www.feedipedia.org/node/23099 Lupins are mainly consumed as fermented foods, bread and pasta products, milk products or sprouts. As of 2020, only 4% of lupin were consumed by humans, with the majority used as [[stock feed]]. [[Lupin beans]] are growing in use as a plant-based protein source in the world marketplace.{{Cite web |date=2020-09-07 |title=Strong Growth Predicted for Lupin Protein Market as Demand for Plant-Based Foods Increases |url=https://vegconomist.com/market-and-trends/strong-growth-predicted-for-lupin-protein-market-as-demand-for-plant-based-foods-increases/ |access-date=2021-02-27 |website=vegconomist}}{{cite journal|last=Sujak|first=Agniesszka |author2=Kotlarz, Anna |author3=Strobel, Waclaw|title=Compositional and nutritional evaluation of several lupin seeds|journal=Food Chemistry|year=2006|volume=98|issue=4|pages=711–719|doi=10.1016/j.foodchem.2005.06.036 |bibcode=2006FoodC..98..711S }} ==Genomics== This species of lupin had its [[genome]] sequenced in May 2013. It was sequenced due to the interest in low [[alkaloid]] mutants as a food crop. ''L. angustifolius'' has a protein content of 35–40% in the seeds thus for providing protein to people of the world it is of high interest. Currently lupin is grown in Australia and sold under the name "Australian sweet lupin". The objective was to figure out how [[agronomic]] traits, low alkaloid traits, and protein content are manifested in the genome. The genome was sequenced in two [[cultivar]]s, the poorly adapted tanjil and the better adapted unicrop. The genome was sequenced as such; [[whole genome shotgun sequencing]] dataset for this species with 26.9x (average amount of overlapping scaffolds) coverage of the genome, then NGS-based RAD-sequencing technology was used to obtain 8,244 sequence-defined markers. A total of 4,214 scaffolds from the genome sequence was assembled and aligned with the genetic map.{{cite journal|last1=Yang|first1=Huaan|last2=Tao|first2=Ye|last3=Zheng|first3=Zequn|last4=Zhang|first4=Qisen|last5=Zhou|first5=Gaofeng|last6=Sweetingham|first6=Mark W.|last7=Howieson|first7=John G.|last8=Li|first8=Chengdao|title=Draft Genome Sequence, and a Sequence-Defined Genetic Linkage Map of the Legume Crop Species Lupinus angustifolius L|journal=PLOS ONE|date=29 May 2013|volume=8|issue=5|article-number=e64799|doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0064799|pmid=23734219|pmc=3667174|bibcode=2013PLoSO...864799Y|doi-access=free}} === Breeding Goals === ''Lupinus angustifolius'' is currently subject of multiple breeding programs. Main focusses are a low [[alkaloid]] content, as alkaloids give a bitter taste to the seed and can be poisonous in high amounts.{{Cite journal|author1=Bundesinstitut für Risikobewertung |title=Alkaloide und Allergien: Aktuelle Datenlage zu gesundheitlichen Risiken durch Lupinensamen in Lebensmitteln: Aktualisierte Stellungnahme Nr. 035/2025 des BfR vom 17. September 2025|url=https://www.openagrar.de/receive/openagrar_mods_00109899|journal=BFR-Stellungnahmen|date=2025-09-17|volume=2025|issue=35|doi=10.17590/20250917-091537-0|language=en}}{{Cite journal |last1=Czepiel|first1=Katarzyna|last2=Krajewski|first2=Paweł|last3=Wilczura|first3=Paulina|last4=Bielecka|first4=Patrycja|last5=Święcicki|first5=Wojciech|last6=Kroc|first6=Magdalena|date=2021-03-06|title=Expression Profiles of Alkaloid-Related Genes across the Organs of Narrow-Leafed Lupin (Lupinus angustifolius L.) and in Response to Anthracnose Infection|journal=International Journal of Molecular Sciences|language=en|volume=22|issue=5|page=2676|doi=10.3390/ijms22052676|doi-access=free |issn=1422-0067|pmc=7962062|pmid=33800929}} In Europe the threshold for human consumption lies at 200 ppm, while it is at 500 ppm for animal feed.{{Cite web |title=FiBL -
